item.title: Return
item.content:encoded:
Hi, everyone. Thanks for the reviews, both good and bad.

I'm back, seven years later, and I'm gonna clean this up. Voct is the real hero of this article, but I think I've come along far enough as a writer that I can salvage my own high school-aged drivel.

Huge thanks to the people who liked this. I've been going through a lot recently, and it's nice to know that not all my ideas are terrible, even when the implementation isn't spot-on.

item.content:encoded:
we have several scps that are listed as found in antique stores

I guess it's a pet peeve of mine. I'm more willing to believe "SCP-XXXX was bought by █████ ██████ in an antique store, and came to Foundation attention when [DATA EXPUNGED] a week later." rather than "Agent ████████ bought SCP-XXXX at a flea market and later realized it was anomalous."

The first makes sense to me because the Foundation should be good at spotting reports of weird things happening — and distinguishing the REAL anomalies from the thousands of slightly-weird-sounding things that happen every day.

The latter makes no sense to me — what are the odds that a random Agent runs into an SCP by chance, and why should he be able to spot one that is a seemingly ordinary object when he buys it?

item.title: Salvage
item.content:encoded:
Okay. I think this can be improved if we put some harsh restrictions on what it can do.

The part about how you have to wait five minutes each time before the emotionless voice appears in your head telling you "that… was the wrong choice", that's a good start. And it never provides any other details. You ask "wait, what? What the fuck does that mean?"

… and five minutes later, it says "swearing at the judgmental turtle… was pointless".

It doesn't give you advice, and it doesn't answer your questions. It just judges your actions (very slowly) and tells you when you made a mistake.

It tells you what the better choice was, according to a given criterion. And it always tells you which criterion it has used to make its judgment. That criterion may or may not be helpful.

Also, it's not sentient. It's very intelligent, but there's no mind there.

whenever we try to use it as a very slow Ouija board to ask it about itself ("you should have chosen… the letter 'W'", etc)…

all we get is the phrase "the judgmental turtle tm is for entertainment value only semicolon manufacturers and vendors of the judgmental turtle tm are not responsible for any injuries which may occur as a result of using the judgmental turtle as a planning aid" (or translations thereof).
